summary: Most visitors need a Tanzanian visa, best obtained as an eVisa through the official immigration portal — USD 50 for an ordinary single-entry visa, while US citizens must buy the USD 100 multiple-entry visa. East African Community neighbors and citizens of many Commonwealth and southern African countries enter visa-free, and every foreign visitor must also buy Tanzania's mandatory local inbound travel insurance.

vaccinations.name: Yellow fever
vaccinations.text: A yellow fever vaccination certificate (ICVP) is required if you arrive from, or spent more than 12 hours in transit through, a country with risk of yellow fever transmission — this catches many travelers connecting through Nairobi or Addis Ababa.

vaccinations.name: Malaria prophylaxis
vaccinations.text: There is a risk of malaria in certain areas of Tanzania and at certain times of year. Antimalarial medication may be recommended depending on your itinerary and season — see a health professional, ideally six weeks before travel — and protect yourself from mosquito bites at all times.

travelInsurance.text: All foreign visitors except residents must hold Tanzanian mandatory inbound travel insurance, bought for their first port of entry: from the state National Insurance Corporation (NIC) if they arrive in mainland Tanzania first, or from the Zanzibar Insurance Corporation (ZIC) if they arrive in Zanzibar first. One policy is enough, it covers up to 92 days, other insurance is not accepted in its place, and it can be bought online or on arrival. Visitors without it may be refused entry.

notes: The UK Foreign Office says plastic bags are banned: if you arrive by air you will be asked to hand them over, although zip-lock bags used for airline security are not included.
Canada's travel advice says you must obtain a permit from the Tanzania Civil Aviation Authority to import a drone.

The UK Foreign Office says exporting wildlife items, including horns and seashells, without a certified export permit from the Ministry of Natural Resources and Tourism is illegal, and advises against bringing animal-skin accessories into the country.

payments.text: Canada's travel advice says Tanzanian shillings or US dollars are the preferred method of payment and credit cards are not widely accepted in rural areas; ATMs in the main cities occasionally run out of cash. The UK Foreign Office says US dollars are widely accepted in tourist areas.

safety.text: Tanzania is one of Africa's most-visited safari destinations and the vast majority of trips are trouble-free. Petty theft occurs in Dar es Salaam, Arusha and on Zanzibar beaches — use registered taxis at night and keep valuables out of sight — and the Mozambique border area in the far south should be avoided.

tips.text: Tanzania requires mandatory inbound travel insurance (up to 92 days): from the National Insurance Corporation if you land on the mainland first, or from the Zanzibar Insurance Corporation (USD 44) if you land in Zanzibar first. One policy is enough, your own insurance does not replace it, and it is checked on arrival.
US citizens cannot buy the USD 50 single-entry visa. They are only eligible for the USD 100 multiple-entry visa, valid 12 months.

Visas are issued on arrival at major airports and borders, but lines are long and payment is cash US dollars — the official eVisa at visa.immigration.go.tz is the smoother option; beware lookalike third-party visa sites.
The UK Foreign Office says plastic bags are banned in Tanzania and air arrivals are asked to hand them over; zip-lock bags for airline security are not included in the ban.
The East Africa Tourist Visa covers Kenya, Uganda and Rwanda only. It is not valid for Tanzania, which needs its own visa.

faq.question: Do I need a visa for Tanzania?
faq.answer: Most visitors do. An ordinary single-entry visa costs USD 50 as an eVisa or on arrival. East African Community citizens and nationals of many Commonwealth and southern African countries are visa-exempt, while US citizens must buy the USD 100 multiple-entry visa.

faq.question: Does the Tanzanian visa cover Zanzibar?
faq.answer: Yes — Zanzibar is part of the United Republic of Tanzania, so the same visa covers it. Zanzibar does run its own immigration checks on arrival. All foreign visitors must also hold the mandatory inbound travel insurance, bought once for the first port of entry: from the Zanzibar Insurance Corporation (USD 44) if you arrive in Zanzibar first, or from the National Insurance Corporation if you arrive on the mainland first.

faq.question: Can I get a Tanzanian visa on arrival?
faq.answer: For most nationalities, yes — at major airports (Dar es Salaam, Kilimanjaro, Zanzibar) and main land borders, paid in cash US dollars. Nationals of the 23 countries on the guidelines' no-visa-on-arrival list (among them Afghanistan, Bangladesh, Iran, Pakistan, Somalia and Syria), stateless people and refugees cannot: they must hold an approved eVisa before travelling. For everyone else the official eVisa at visa.immigration.go.tz is usually the easier route.

faq.question: Why do US citizens pay more for a Tanzanian visa?
faq.answer: Under a reciprocal arrangement, US passport holders are only eligible for the multiple-entry visa at USD 100 (valid 12 months). The USD 50 single-entry visa is not available to them.

faq.question: Do I need a yellow fever certificate for Tanzania?
faq.answer: Only if you arrive from — or transit more than 12 hours through — a country with yellow fever risk. Direct arrivals from Europe, the Americas or Asia do not need one, but connections through Nairobi or Addis Ababa can trigger the requirement.

faq.question: Is the East Africa Tourist Visa valid for Tanzania?
faq.answer: No — despite the name, the East Africa Tourist Visa covers only Kenya, Uganda and Rwanda. Tanzania requires its own visa or visa exemption.
